prompt: What can a storage account key do?
hint: It is the master key, not a user's password.

choices.text: Read blobs, and nothing else unless a role allows it
choices.why: A key is not limited by roles; it signs any request.

choices.text: Only what the person who listed it is allowed to do
choices.why: The key carries no identity; whoever holds it can do everything.

choices.text: Anything, in the whole account
choices.why: Right. That is why it should never leave the account.

choices.text: Manage the account's settings in Azure Resource Manager
choices.why: Resource Manager is the control plane, behind a login; the key works on the data plane.

prompt: A request signed with a key that differs by one character was refused. What does the account compare?
hint: The key never travels.

choices.text: Its own signature against the one sent
choices.why: Right. Only the HMAC travels.

choices.text: The key sent in the request against the one it stores
choices.why: The key is never sent.

choices.text: The account's network rules against the caller's address
choices.why: That is what the command line suggested, and it was not the cause.

choices.text: The caller's login against the account's roles
choices.why: A key-signed request has no login at all.

prompt: An account key was printed in a public build log an hour ago. What is the first thing to do, and what does it cost?
hint: Nothing records who has a copy.

choices.text: Delete the build log, which removes the key from circulation
choices.why: Anybody who read the log in that hour still has the key.

choices.text: Set the containers to `off`, which blocks the key
choices.why: The public level concerns anonymous requests; a key-signed one ignores it.

choices.text: Wait for the key to expire, which takes seven days
choices.why: Account keys do not expire.

choices.text: Regenerate the key at once, and every client still on it breaks
choices.why: Right. The breakage is the price of having used the key.

prompt: Put Microsoft's documented key rotation in order, starting with every client on `key1`.
hint: Nobody is ever left on a key that is about to change.
items: Move every client back to the new `key1`

prompt: Match each SAS parameter to what it carries.
hint: `echo "$SAS" | tr "&" "\n"` printed them one per line.

prompt: Somebody edits a read-only SAS in the URL, changing `sp=r` to `sp=rw`, and tries a write. What happens?
hint: What does the signature cover?

choices.text: The write succeeds, because `sp` now says `w`
choices.why: `sp` is covered by the signature; changing it invalidates the signature.

choices.text: It is refused: the signature is broken
choices.why: Right. `AuthorizationFailure` in the lab.

choices.text: It is refused with `AuthorizationPermissionMismatch`
choices.why: That is the answer to a valid SAS lacking a permission; this one is no longer valid.

choices.text: Reads keep working and only the write fails
choices.why: The edited URL fails for reads too; the original URL still reads.

prompt: A SAS signed for `exports/2026/10/orders-2026-10-29.csv` is used on the 28 October export in the same container. Why is it refused?
hint: `sr=b`.

choices.text: The 28th has expired
choices.why: The expiry belongs to the SAS, not to the blob it is used on.

choices.text: Its signature covers the path of one blob
choices.why: Right. `sr=b` and the path are part of what was signed.

choices.text: A SAS works once and was already used
choices.why: A SAS works as many times as wanted until it expires.

choices.text: Reading another blob needs `l` as well as `r`
choices.why: `l` lists a container; it does not widen a blob SAS to other blobs.

prompt: Which kind of SAS keeps working after shared key access is switched off for the account?
hint: Which one is not signed with the account key?

choices.text: A service SAS signed against a stored access policy
choices.why: It is still signed with the account key, and shared key is off.

choices.text: An account SAS
choices.why: Also signed with the account key.

choices.text: None; switching shared key off ends every SAS
choices.why: The user delegation SAS is the exception, by design.

choices.text: A user delegation SAS
choices.why: Right. It is signed with a key Entra ID issued.

prompt: For how many days at most is a user delegation key valid, according to Microsoft's documentation?
hint: A week.

prompt: The SAS made from the `analysts` policy had no `sp` and no `se`. Where are the permissions and the expiry?
hint: `si=analysts`.

choices.text: In the policy, stored on the container
choices.why: Right. The SAS names it with `si`.

choices.text: In the account key
choices.why: The key signs; it holds no permissions.

choices.text: Nowhere: such a SAS grants everything until revoked
choices.why: It grants what the policy says, `rl` until its expiry.

choices.text: In the signature, encoded
choices.why: A signature proves; it carries nothing readable.

prompt: Quitanda deletes the `analysts` policy. What happens to the SAS URLs already handed out with it?
hint: The lab used the same URL before and after.

choices.text: They keep working until their own expiry
choices.why: They have no expiry of their own; it was the policy's.

choices.text: They stop only after the account key is rotated
choices.why: Deleting the policy is enough; that is its purpose.

choices.text: They stop working at once
choices.why: Right. The lab's listing was refused right after the delete.

choices.text: They become read-only
choices.why: They become nothing at all.

prompt: How many stored access policies can one container hold, according to Microsoft's documentation?
hint: Fewer than ten.

prompt: A partner needs read access to one container for a month, and Quitanda wants to be able to cut it off the day the contract ends early. Which SAS?
hint: Which one can be taken back without rotating the key?

choices.text: A service SAS with `--expiry` a month away
choices.why: Only rotating the key would end it early.

choices.text: An account SAS for a month
choices.why: Wider than needed, and just as hard to take back.

choices.text: A public container, with the URL sent only to the partner
choices.why: Public means anybody, whoever the URL was sent to.

choices.text: One signed against a policy for the partner
choices.why: Right. Deleting the policy ends it the same day.

prompt: With the container's level at `blob`, what can a request with no credentials do?
hint: The lab tried two things.

choices.text: List the container, and not read the blobs
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: Read and list, since the container is public
choices.why: Listing needs the level `container`.

choices.text: Read a blob by its name, and not list
choices.why: Right. The listing was refused at that level.

choices.text: Nothing, until a SAS is added
choices.why: `curl` read the export with no SAS at all.

prompt: Why is `blob` level not safe for Quitanda's exports, even though nobody can list them?
hint: How were the names chosen in lesson 2?

choices.text: `blob` level also allows writes
choices.why: Public levels only ever allow reading.

choices.text: Their names follow a guessable pattern
choices.why: Right. A lake's names are predictable by design.

choices.text: Search engines index public blobs automatically
choices.why: The lesson did not claim that; guessable names are enough.

choices.text: The level expires after a day and turns into `container`
choices.why: Levels do not change on their own.

prompt: On Azure, a container's level says `container`, and the account's `allowBlobPublicAccess` is false. What does an anonymous listing get?
hint: Which of the two settings wins?

choices.text: A refusal
choices.why: Right. With the account switch false, no container is public.

choices.text: The list of names, as the container allows
choices.why: The account's false wins over any container level.

choices.text: Only the blobs written before the switch was set
choices.why: The switch applies to every request, whatever the blob's age.

choices.text: The names, without the content
choices.why: No anonymous request gets anything.

prompt: Match each leak to the setting that removes it.
hint: One line of `main.tf` each.

pairs.left: a container set to public for a test
an account key committed with code
a SAS signed for a year

prompt: Which column of `StorageBlobLogs` tells an anonymous read from a read signed with a SAS?
hint: It names how the request was authenticated.

choices.text: `OperationName`
choices.why: It says what was done, `GetBlob`, not how it was signed.

choices.text: `Uri`
choices.why: It says which blob; a SAS can sit in the query string of either.

choices.text: `AuthenticationType`
choices.why: Right. Anonymous, SAS, key or Entra ID.

choices.text: `StatusCode`
choices.why: Both reads succeed with 200.

prompt: Quitanda switches shared key access off. Which of its programs from lessons 2 to 5 stop working, and why?
hint: How does `UseDevelopmentStorage=true` sign?

choices.text: All of them: each signs with the key
choices.why: Right. They would need an Entra ID identity instead.

choices.text: None; they use the Python library, which signs with Entra ID
choices.why: The library signs with whatever the connection string gives it: here, the key.

choices.text: Only the ones that write; reads keep working
choices.why: The switch refuses key-signed reads too.

choices.text: Only the ones that use `az`
choices.why: The libraries and `az` sign the same way here.

prompt: A SAS used for a write it does not grant is refused with the error code ___.
hint: Authorization, then permission, then mismatch.

prompt: Which of these revoke a leaked service SAS before its expiry? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does the signature depend on?

choices.text: Regenerating the account key that signed it
choices.why: Yes, and every other client using that key breaks too.

choices.text: Deleting the stored access policy it names, if it names one
choices.why: Yes; the lab's listing failed right after the delete.

choices.text: Setting the container's public access level to `off`
choices.why: A SAS is not anonymous access; the level does not affect it.

choices.text: Deleting the blob and uploading it again
choices.why: The SAS names the path, so it reads the new blob just as well.
